$comment: closeout's capability matrix against the three packages it replaces (compat-oracle's LAYERS). Rendered by <CapabilityMatrix pkg="closeout" /> from apps/docs-chassis and held by scripts/capabilities-lock.test.ts: every `ours` yes/partial names a test file and a title substring it contains, or a compat-oracle grade; every incumbent cell names a source at the version compat-oracle grades, and a local source is checked for the text it `quote`s or `lacks`. `n/a` means the row does not apply to that package, and says why. A row that could not be proved for every column is not here.

rows.capability: One registry for every exit path
rows.why: A handler registered once runs on a signal, an uncaught throw, an unhandled rejection, an emptied event loop (`beforeExit`) and `process.exit()`, so no door out skips the cleanup.

ours.title: every door out leaves the terminal as it was found, last

signal-exit.missing: no `beforeExit` trigger, so an async handler never gets the emptied loop's time; a throw or a rejection reaches handlers only through the `exit` event behind it

exit-hook.missing: no SIGHUP, SIGQUIT, uncaughtException or unhandledRejection listener; a throw reaches only the synchronous hooks, through `exit`

restore-cursor.note: registers one handler of its own, the cursor restore, and takes none of yours

rows.capability: The handler is told which door, and what was thrown
rows.why: Every handler gets `{ path, signal, code, error }`, so it can tell Ctrl-C from a crash and keep the temp directory for a bug report.

ours.title: tells a handler which door the program left by

signal-exit.note: a handler gets `(code, signal)`; a throw arrives as code 1 with no error

exit-hook.note: a hook gets the exit code alone

rows.capability: Exactly once when two doors fire together
rows.why: Ctrl-C twice, or a signal and the `exit` behind it, is one shutdown, so a lock is never released twice.

ours.title: runs a handler once however many times shutdown is asked for

restore-cursor.note: registers once, and signal-exit's emitter runs the handler once

rows.capability: One handler's throw does not skip the rest
rows.why: A handler that throws is reported and the handlers after it still run, so the one that restores the terminal is not the one that gets skipped.

ours.title: runs the rest after one throws, and reports it

signal-exit.note: calls each handler in a plain loop; a throw ends the loop, and the handlers after it do not run

exit-hook.note: calls each synchronous hook in a plain loop; a throw ends the loop

restore-cursor.note: runs one handler of its own

rows.capability: A deadline that names the handler that hung
rows.why: A handler that never returns cannot hold Ctrl-C hostage: after the deadline (2000 ms by default) the process leaves with the code it was leaving with and prints which handlers had not returned.

ours.title: does not stop a signal from ending the process, and is named in the report

signal-exit.note: awaits nothing a handler returns, so an async cleanup is abandoned rather than bounded

exit-hook.missing: each async hook carries its own `wait`, the longest one bounds the rest, and the forced exit names no hook

restore-cursor.note: one synchronous write; nothing to bound

rows.capability: Phases: flush, release, then restore last
rows.why: Handlers run in `flush`, `release`, `restore` order, each phase awaited before the next, so the terminal comes back after the log is written whichever registered first.

ours.title: runs the handler before the restore, though the restore was registered first

signal-exit.missing: two tiers, `exit` then `afterExit`, in registration order within each; nothing is awaited between them

exit-hook.note: registration order, every synchronous hook before any asynchronous one

restore-cursor.missing: its one restore goes last through signal-exit's `alwaysLast`; there are no phases for anything else

rows.capability: The restore still runs after a handler hung
rows.why: Past the deadline the later phases are still run, just no longer waited for, so a hung `flush` does not decide that the cursor stays hidden.

ours.title: still runs restore after a handler hung in flush

signal-exit.note: has no deadline to run past

exit-hook.missing: every async hook is started at once, so a restore hook does run, but beside the hung one rather than after it

restore-cursor.note: has no deadline to run past

rows.capability: Cursor, raw mode and the alternate screen restored
rows.why: `hideCursor`, `rawMode` and `alternateScreen` make the change and register its undo in the `restore` phase, so a full-screen program that dies by any door hands back a usable terminal.

ours.title: turns raw mode off when the program exits without turning it off

signal-exit.note: writes nothing to a terminal; the restore is a handler you write

exit-hook.note: writes nothing to a terminal; the restore is a hook you write

restore-cursor.missing: the cursor only; raw mode and the alternate screen are left as they were

rows.capability: A second signal waits for the first shutdown
rows.why: A second Ctrl-C, or a SIGTERM behind it, while a handler still holds the first shutdown waits for that shutdown, so the restore runs before the process dies.

ours.title: the terminal a real process leaves behind (R4)

signal-exit.note: handlers run synchronously inside the first signal's listener, so no second signal arrives mid-shutdown

exit-hook.note: the listener is `once`: a second SIGINT while an async hook runs finds none, and the process dies there

restore-cursor.note: one synchronous write inside signal-exit's handler

rows.capability: No escape sequences into a pipe
rows.why: A stream that is not a terminal gets no cursor or screen sequence on the way in or out, so a log carries only what the program wrote.

ours.title: writes nothing to a pipe, in either direction

rows.capability: A signalled process dies of the signal
rows.why: After the handlers run, the signal is re-raised, so a shell prints `^C`, `make` stops, and a CI runner marks the job cancelled rather than failed.

ours.title: a signal that nobody else claimed still kills the process

exit-hook.note: exits 128 + n, so a parent sees an exit code, not a signal; `closeout/exit-hook` keeps that, as exit-hook's suite requires

restore-cursor.note: through signal-exit, which it depends on

rows.capability: A program that owns the signal keeps it
rows.why: When the program has its own listener for the signal, the handlers run and the program still decides what happens next, with one delivery for one Ctrl-C.

ours.title: runs the handlers and then stands down, leaving the exit to the program

exit-hook.note: exits after the hooks, whatever other listeners the program has

restore-cursor.note: through signal-exit, which it depends on

rows.capability: The shutdown as one `--json` line or an agent event
rows.why: `reportToJson()` and `reportToEvent()` project the record the handlers were given, with `timedOut` and the handlers that hung, so a log and an agent read the same facts.

ours.title: is one line and names every handler that hung

rows.capability: Plugins: named handlers in a phase, readable as data
rows.why: A plugin contributes named handlers to `flush` or `release`, is validated against the family schema, and `contributions()` lists the whole shutdown in order without running it.

ours.title: projects the shutdown sequence as data

rows.why: `closeout/exit-hook` is graded by exit-hook 5.1.0's own tests, unedited, so changing the import keeps exit-hook's behaviour, 128 + n exit codes included.
